# The explicit simplex scalar correction also controls complementary caps

Together with `candidate 1f9aa6ef8c94292a`, this proves
that one scalar multiple of the ordinary centroid corrects every
vertex-isolating centroidal simplex section in both orientations. It
does not address other section types or general convex bodies.

## 1. Statement and reduction

Let d≥2 and λ_i∈(0,1/d] sum to1. Use the explicit c in the preceding
note. Then every corrected vertex-cap fraction Q_i=p_i−c s_i obeys

    γ_d ≤ Q_i ≤ 5/9 ≤ 1−γ_d.                         (1)

The first inequality was proved in that note. The last follows because
γ_d≤γ_2=4/9 for d≥2. For completeness the monotonicity follows from
(d/dx)[x log(x/(x+1))]=log(1−1/(x+1))+1/(x+1)<0.

Put s_j=dλ_j, a=min s_j, b=max s_j, and omit chosen minimum and
maximum indices to obtain the remaining set R. Thus s_j∈(0,1],
Σs_j=d, and

    D=d+1−Σ_{j∈R}1/s_j>0.

For an omitted index Q_i=Π_R s_j/D; the proof below also includes
these endpoint cases using the minimum of the same quadratic. For i∈R the preceding note gives

    Q_i=(Π_R s_j/D)[(a+b)/s_i−ab/s_i²].               (2)

Keep the remaining coordinates fixed. Then a+b=d−Σ_R s_j≥1, and
(2) decreases as ab increases. Its maximum over feasible a,b is
therefore at b=1 and a=d−1−Σ_R s_j: expanding the two extrema while
preserving their sum respects a≤s_j≤b. If the new a is zero, all
remaining s_j equal1, and the limiting value is1/2. We can otherwise
assume a>0.

Write x_j=1−s_j for j∈R, choose t=x_i, and denote the other x values
by y_1,...,y_N, where N=d−2. Then

    a=t+Y,    Y=Σ y_j,
    t≥0, y_j≥0,    t+Y+max(t,y_1,...,y_N)≤1.          (3)

Formula(2) becomes

    Q= Π_j(1−y_j)(A−tY)
         /[B−(1−t)Σ_j y_j/(1−y_j)],                 (4)

where A=1−t−t² and B=2−3t. For N=0 this is A/B. The goal is Q≤5/9.
All denominators are positive: writing m=1−t−Y, (3) says every
variable is at most m and their sum is1−m. Hence
Σ x/(1−x)≤1 and the corresponding D=2−Σx/(1−x) is at least1.
Also A−tY=1−t−t(t+Y)≥(1−t)²>0.

## 2. Spreading the other variables

Fix t,Y. Set m=1−t−Y. The other variables lie in the compact polytope
0≤y_j≤m, Σy_j=Y. Holding two of them at fixed sum z and product p,
(4), up to a positive constant, equals

    (1−z+p)² /
    [B_0(1−z+p)−(1−t)(z−2p)],

where B_0≤B includes the contributions of the untouched variables.
The derivative with respect to p has the sign of

    E=(B_0−2(1−t))(1−z)
       +(B_0+2(1−t))p−2(1−t)z.

Using 0≤t≤1/2,0≤z≤1,p≤z²/4, and B_0≤2−3t, gives

    E≤−t(1−z)+(4−5t)z²/4−2(1−t)z
      ≤−t(1−z)+(−1+3t/4)z≤0.

Thus making two interior variables more unequal increases Q. Repeating
until one reaches0 or m leaves at most one variable strictly between
the bounds. It suffices to consider k variables equal m, one residual
r∈[0,m], and zeros. They satisfy

    (k+1)m+r=1−t,       m≥t.                         (5)

A zero residual can always be added as a dummy zero variable; it
cancels from the formulas below.

## 3. Reducing every k≥1 to k=1

Fix t,r and allow real k≥1 in the feasible range. Put

    z=1−t−r, m=z/(k+1), u=1−m, h=1−t, v=1−r.

Then

    Q_k= [u^k v(h−tu)]/[hD_k],
    D_k=k+4−1/h−k/u−1/v≥1.                          (6)

The bound on D_k follows exactly as after(4), allowing the k identical
variables with positive real multiplicity. When k decreases toward1,
conditions t,r≤m remain valid.

The factor v(h−tu)/h decreases as k increases. It remains to show that
u^k/D_k decreases. Set w=z/(k+1). A direct differentiation gives

    −(log u^k)'=w²/[z(1−w)]−L(w),
    −D_k'=w²(1−z)/[z(1−w)²],
    L(w)=log(1−w)+w/(1−w).

Here0<w≤z/2 and0<z≤1. The power series, or integration of its
nonnegative derivative, gives

    L(w)≤w²/[2(1−w)²],      0≤w<1.

Since D_k≥1, subtraction yields

    −(log u^k)'−(−D_k'/D_k)
       ≥ w²(z−w)/[z(1−w)²]−L(w)≥0.

Thus Q_k≤Q_1. In particular it suffices to prove Q_1≤1/2.

## 4. An exact polynomial certificate for Q_1≤1/2

For k=1, m=(1−t−r)/2, and the domain is the quadrilateral

    t,r≥0,       3t+r≤1,       t+3r≤1.               (7)

Set u=(1+t+r)/2,h=1−t,v=1−r. Let N=u v(h−tu)/h and
D=5−1/h−1/u−1/v. Then Q_1=N/D, D≥1, and

    D−2N=P(t,r)/[2(1−r)(1−t)(1+t+r)],

where

    P=t⁴(r−1)²
      +t³(3r³−r²−7r+5)
      +t²(3r⁴+4r³−12r²+10r−3)
      +t(r⁵+3r⁴−6r³+8r²−5r+1)
      −2r⁴−4r²+2r.

The following coefficient identity certifies P≥0 on(7). Split(7)
into the two triangles with common vertices(0,0),(1/4,1/4) and third
vertices(1/3,0) or(0,1/3). For nonnegative U,V,W, set H=U+V+W and

    A(U,V,W)=41472 H⁶ P((U/3+V/4)/H,(V/4)/H),
    B(U,V,W)=124416 H⁶ P((V/4)/H,(U/3+V/4)/H).

Expanding gives the following coefficients of U^i V^j W^k. The
coefficient of W⁶ is0; every other degree-six monomial is listed.
All coefficients are nonnegative.

This is a finite polynomial identity and a positivity proof, not a
numerical test. It gives P≥0 on both triangles, and hence Q_1≤1/2.

## 5. The remaining k=0 case

There is only one nonzero other variable y, and

    Q(t,y)=(1−y)²(A−ty)/[B−Cy],   C=3−4t,
    0≤t≤1/2,
    0≤y≤min((1−t)/2,1−2t).

For fixed t, this is convex in y. Polynomial division gives a quadratic
quotient with leading coefficient t/C and remainder

    R=(1−t)²(2t−1)(2t²+3t−3)/C³≥0.

Thus Q_yy=2t/C+2C²R/(B−Cy)³≥0. Its maximum occurs at an endpoint.
At y=0,

    5/9−Q(t,0)=(3t−1)²/[9(2−3t)]≥0.

If t≤1/3, the other endpoint is y=(1−t)/2. This is exactly the
k=1 configuration with residual0, already bounded by1/2. If t≥1/3,
the other endpoint is y=1−2t. Direct substitution gives

    Q(t,1−2t)−1/2
      =−(2t−1)(4t³−6t²+5t−1)/[2(8t²−7t+1)]≤0.

Indeed the quadratic denominator is negative on[1/3,1/2], while the
cubic is positive there: its derivative is12(t−1/2)²+2 and its value
at1/3 is4/27. This proves Q≤5/9 in every case.

For an omitted minimum or maximum index, Q is the minimum of the
concave quadratic in the previous note. Choose any remaining index
and apply its upper bound to obtain Q_end≤5/9, sufficient for(1).
The stronger endpoint bound1/2 mentioned above is not needed.

The upper constant5/9 is attained for every d≥2 by scaled coordinates
(s_0,s_1,s_2,s_3,...,s_d)=(1/3,1,2/3,1,...,1), choosing the cap at s_i=2/3.
For d=2 this is λ=(1/6,1/2,1/3). Complementing gives corrected fraction4/9.

## 6. Consequence and exact scope

For every vertex-side or complementary centroidal simplex cap,

    capfraction−c[S(u·g)/|T|] ≥ γ_d.

Therefore their weighted average is at least γ_d whenever only the
scalar balance Σθ_i S_i(u_i·g)=0 holds. This is stronger than full-normal
balance for this restricted section family. It supplies no inequality
for a quadrilateral tetrahedral section or any other non-vertex section.
